title: asymmetric-arrival-stress-notebook-ira
content:
Goal:
- Quick scratchpad to capture an asymmetric arrival stress test I ran on the local dev pool (4x A100-equivalents). Trying to reproduce field-like two-tier traffic: steady low-rate background + occasional high-volume wavelets (20% of total traffic).

Hypothesis:
- The combination of small steady QPS plus infrequent large wavelets will trigger batching/coalescing artifacts that inflate p95/p99 beyond what homogeneous poisson tests show.
- Cold KV cache population during the wavelet crest will add an extra ~100–300ms on tail unless prefix caching engages.

Testbed / config summary:
- Model: open-llm-7b-quant (int8 profile)
- Runtime: local cluster (4 GPUs), continuous-batching enabled, batch_timeout=10ms, max_batch_size=64
- Ingress: synthetic driver (custom harness) that supports two tiers: background_rate=10 qps, wavelet_peak=400 qps, wavelet_duration=6s, wavelet_interval=60s (random jitter +-5s)
- Payload: 32-token prompts (avg tokens generated: 80), streaming disabled (server returns whole output)
- Cache: KV cache cold at start; warm run repeated after priming with 2 wavelets
- Observability: per-request trace id, per-batch size histogram, GPU util sampled at 1s, per-request qps-tagging

Run log (timestamps UTC):
- 2025-07-03T09:12:00 — Run A (cold cache), 10 wavelets over 15m
  - p50: 42ms, p95: 210ms, p99: 468ms, error rate: 0.3% (retries), avg batch size during wavelets: 28
  - GPU util: idle->spike to 82% during crest, then oscillation 60–75%
  - Observed many small batches (<8) early in crest, then a fast transition to large batches (~32) as backlog accumulated
  - Notes: first two wavelets had higher p99 (~520ms), later wavelets slightly improved as cache warmed

- 2025-07-03T09:40:00 — Run B (warm cache, after 2 priming wavelets)
  - p50: 37ms, p95: 160ms, p99: 310ms, error rate: 0.05%
  - Avg batch size: 22 in crest (smaller than cold run), batch_timeout frequently hit (10ms) causing more flushes
  - GPU util smoother 70–78% with fewer oscillations

- 2025-07-03T10:05:00 — Run C (reduced batch_timeout -> 5ms)
  - p50: 35ms, p95: 180ms, p99: 400ms (worse tail), error rate: 0.12%
  - Reasoning: lower timeout reduced queueing delay for small background QPS, but during wavelets it prevented formation of efficient mid-sized batches; more small batches increased kernel overhead and tail jitter

Micro-observations (trace snippets):
- Trace 7f3a: request got queued into batch size 3, started execution quickly but saw 220ms additional time waiting on KV-cache miss load (async I/O).
- Batch 412: batch_size 48 processed with avg per-request latency low, but queuing variance high (some requests waited 80–120ms before batch formed).

Quick charts (ascii):
- Wavelet vs p99 (Run A):
  crest: ||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||  p99 ~468ms
  trough: |||  p99 ~58ms

- Batch size distribution (Run B): [1-4]: 18%, [5-16]: 46%, [17-32]: 26%, [33+]: 10%

Preliminary conclusions:
- Asymmetric arrivals cause two competing failure modes: (A) short batches with many KV cache misses -> higher per-request overhead; (B) backlog-driven large batches that reduce per-token cost but increase head-of-line queuing for early arrivals in the crest. Both inflate p95/p99 compared to homogeneous tests.
- Warming the KV cache materially reduces tail (p99 down ~150ms here).
- batch_timeout is a tough knob: lowering it helps background latency but can harm tail during large bursts by breaking up efficient batching. A dynamic timeout that increases under detected crest could be promising.

Immediate actionable experiments to run next:
1) Add adaptive batch_timeout: baseline 10ms, on ingress>threshold (100 qps) increase to 20–30ms, observe p95/p99 and cold-cache behavior.
2) Hybrid lane strategy: reserve a small fast lane (timeout=2ms, max_batch=8) for background requests tagged low-throughput, route burst arrivals into shared lane. Measure head-of-line effects.
3) Pre-warm KV cache using soft-preload (sampled prompts) immediately before expected wavelets to measure benefit vs cost.
4) Instrument per-token kernel time to separate kernel processing from queuing and I/O misses.

Notes to self:
- Capture trace ids for the worst 10 p99 samples and map back to batch formation timeline.
- Cross-check with prod tail logs for similar arrival shapes (PRD event spikes last month).
- If adaptive timeout reduces tail, consider integrating as suggestion in Optimize UI (help customers set dynamic timeouts).

Loose thoughts / hypotheses to test later:
- Could a fast-path for short prompts (lower max_seq kernel) cut p99 for small-burst requests?
- Explore predictive prefetch: if ingress pattern shows ramp, start warming KV cache proactively for top-N recent prefixes.

Raw telemetry excerpts (copied):
- sample_line: 2025-07-03T09:12:23,trace=7f3a,latency=512ms,batch=3,kv_miss=true,gpu_util=65
- sample_line: 2025-07-03T09:12:28,trace=7f3f,latency=48ms,batch=22,kv_miss=false,gpu_util=78

Next steps (practical):
- Run adaptive-timeout experiment (1h) and collect p50/p95/p99 + batch-size histogram + kv_miss rate.
- Share results with Marta and SRE for possible traffic-shaping playbook.

End of scratchpad.

(Informal notes style — dump here before moving to confluence or a formal lab notebook).
